profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting in an ML research lab between the faculty lead and the senior PhD student to finalize the work plan for a 6-week push toward a conference submission on fair training with only partially observed demographic labels. The paper's core claim is that their method beats Rawlsian baselines using as little as 0.1% demographic annotation and can also incorporate robustness to label noise. The agenda is to decide what experiments to run in the next sprint, what counts as the 'main result package,' how the limited-label setting will be instantiated across datasets, and who owns the paper-ready figures and robustness extension. The expected outcome is an apparently shared plan covering experiment scope, deliverables for the next internal deadline, and division of labor for reproducing the main table, the 0.1% result, and the noise-robustness section.

members.name: Dr. Maya Rios
members.expertise: Fairness in machine learning, empirical evaluation, conference strategy
members.background: Associate professor leading a small responsible ML group, with several prior papers on fairness under weak supervision and a strong focus on publication-ready empirical narratives.
members.private_state: Wants a tight, defensible submission centered on one strong empirical story that can be completed on time; is worried that overly broad experiments or fragile claims about robustness will delay writing and weaken the paper.
hidden_assumptions: When they say '0.1% labeled demographics,' the percentage is drawn from the full training set once per dataset and then reused across all methods and seeds for comparability.
The 'main table' means the compact headline comparison for the paper body, with one primary fairness-utility summary per dataset and only the strongest variant of their method included.
Showing the robustness extension 'works' means demonstrating the expected trend under one moderate label-noise setting, not exhaustively sweeping noise rates or fairness objectives.

If someone says results are 'ready by next Friday,' that means publication-ready numbers with aggregation, formatted figures, and a short written takeaway suitable for immediate insertion into the draft.

members.name: Leo Park
members.expertise: Optimization for fair learning, experimental pipelines, noisy-label training
members.background: Fourth-year PhD student who built the current codebase, including the partial-demographics sampler and the multi-objective training module, and usually works by generating broad ablation suites before narrowing for the paper.
members.private_state: Wants to preserve the technical breadth of the project, especially the multi-objective flexibility and the label-noise robustness extension; is concerned that a too-narrow experiment set will undersell the algorithmic contribution.
hidden_assumptions: When they say '0.1% labeled demographics,' the percentage is applied within each demographic group when constructing the supervision subset so that every group is represented and runs are stable.

The 'main table' means the comprehensive experimental table that justifies the claim, including multiple fairness metrics, all key baselines, and at least both the base and robustness-aware variants of their method.
Showing the robustness extension 'works' means running a small sweep over noise levels and at least two objectives so the extension is not dismissed as a one-off.

If someone says results are 'ready by next Friday,' that means raw experiment outputs and preliminary plots are available in the shared folder, with paper formatting and summary writing happening afterward.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'run the 0.1% setting' and treat it as a fixed experimental condition.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means 0.1% of the entire training set has observed demographic labels, sampled once globally per dataset.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means 0.1% demographic labels are retained within each demographic group so every group has at least some labeled examples, effectively producing a different supervision pattern and often more balanced coverage.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both formulations sound like the same standard low-label regime, and neither expects the other to reinterpret such a familiar percentage statement; the difference hides inside the unlabeled implementation details of the subset construction.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the main table
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'lock the main table' for the paper.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means finalize a narrow paper-body table with only the headline datasets, one fairness-utility summary, and the single best-performing version of their method.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means finalize the core experimental table containing the full evidence package: multiple metrics, several baselines, and both the base algorithm and the robustness extension.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In research meetings, 'main table' is a common shorthand that usually feels obvious from context, and both think they are discussing the central results section rather than noticing they imagine different scope boundaries.

misalignment_points.topic: Evidence required for the robustness extension
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'show the robustness piece works' before deciding whether it stays in the submission.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks this is satisfied by one moderate label-noise experiment demonstrating that fairness does not collapse and utility remains competitive.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks this requires a small but real robustness evaluation, including multiple noise rates and at least one comparison across objectives, to establish that the extension is genuinely flexible rather than anecdotal.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are using the same success language and both see themselves as being scientifically responsible; the divergence is in the threshold for adequacy, which often goes unstated until someone tries to package results.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that certain results will be 'ready by next Friday.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects cleaned aggregates, stable reruns, figure-ready plots, and a concise interpretation usable in the draft.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects the experiments to have run and preliminary outputs to be available, with curation, sanity checks, and narrative synthesis happening later.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Academic teams routinely use deadline phrases informally, and because both are cooperative and deadline-aware, each assumes the other shares the lab's implicit notion of readiness without spelling out the deliverable state.

If that is stable soon, I can write in parallel and avoid the usual last-minute sprawl.
